title.en: Nine Gold Medals: a poem by David Roth
When a race becomes a lesson in kindness

text.en: Races are usually about who comes first. This poem tells a true-style story of a race where something more important than winning happened.

Nine Gold Medals is a narrative poem by David Roth. A narrative poem tells a story, and this one has eight stanzas.
Athletes from all over the country have trained for weeks and months to race in a hundred-yard dash. The spectators gather and excitement is high.
Nine resolved athletes wait at the starting blocks. When the pistol fires, the runners charge ahead.
The smallest runner stumbles, falls to the asphalt and cries out in frustration, because his dreams and efforts seem dashed.
The other eight runners stop, turn back and help him to his feet. This is the turning point of the poem.
All nine then join hands and walk to the finish line. A banner above reads Special Olympics, which fits the spirit of the moment.
The race ends with nine gold medals, a standing ovation and nine beaming faces. The poet says those faces say more than words can.
The theme is that compassion and teamwork matter more than winning. The mood moves from excitement to anxiety to joy.

problem.en: Describe how the mood changes in the poem.

text.en: It starts with excitement as the race begins.
It turns anxious when the smallest runner falls.
It ends in joy when all finish together.

prompt.en: Why are the medals called gold for all nine runners?

requiredIdeas.en: The event was the Special Olympics
